kurz: A p package is a small, clearly checkable task that a fresh `claude -p` worker does alongside the interactive agents. The lead plans it so that AMW can start it, check it and present it for approval without asking: with an acceptance command, narrow areas and the details of what to work with.
brauchst: A task that can be finished on its own – small, without visual design and without decisions a person has to see.
A command that is red today and turns green once the task is done.
The lead role (or the person): only whoever plans sets package details.

schritte.text: Good fits: a bug with a clear test, a small extension in a few files, text or docs with a checkable result. Not a fit: anything needing the screen, a GPU, a lot of memory, visual design or open questions – that stays with an interactive agent.

A command AMW runs itself, e.g. `python -m unittest tests.test_calculator`. It must be red **before** the work – otherwise it checks nothing, and AMW does not start the package. A dedicated new test is usually the best acceptance command.

Only the files or patterns the package may really change, e.g. `amw/calculator.py,tests/test_calculator.py`. Anything outside counts as a deviation after the run. Two packages with overlapping areas do not run at the same time.

`amw aufgabe neu --titel … --paket p --pruefbefehl "python -m unittest tests.test_calculator" --dateien amw/calculator.py,tests/test_calculator.py --bogen <no>` – or switch an existing task with `amw aufgabe aendern <no> --paket p …`. If something is missing, AMW says so right away as “Achtung”.
`amw paket zeigen <no>` shows all details, defaults included. When everything is right, `amw paket zustand <no> startklar` releases the package for starting.

werte: `p` for a `claude -p` worker; `agent` (default) for an existing interactive agent; `sitzung` for a new session
the acceptance command – required for `p`, red before the work
the areas – required for `p`, as narrow as possible
like `claude --model` / `--effort`; default claude-opus-5-5 and high, medium is often enough for simple packages
leicht (light, default) / schwer (heavy); gpu, bildschirm (screen) – AMW does not start a p package that is heavy or needs resources
never at the same time as these tasks, e.g. `A12,A13`
a name; packages with the same name run one after the other
`normal` (default); `test-schreiben`: a test for a change (red against the old state); `test-ergaenzen`: only tests for existing code (green, test files only)
fehler: AMW does not start the package like this. Add `--pruefbefehl` or `--dateien`.
“Achtung: Art p mit Gewicht schwer oder Ressourcen”
A p package only runs light and without GPU or screen. Either cut it smaller or give it to an interactive agent with `--paket agent`.
The change is not allowed; the message lists which states are possible from here.
Another agent tried to set package details. The lead plans those.
danach: **Follow it in the Workbench:** Work › Packages shows every package with type, state, cost and – if it does not start – the reason in words (e.g. “Does not start: all workspaces in use”). For “waiting for lead/you” it says whose turn it is. On the PC you can move a package up or defer it, pause all new starts, watch a running worker with “Follow along” and end it with its sub-processes using “Emergency stop” – every intervention is in the planning log. Online and on the phone you only see the list; control happens on the PC. “What do the states mean?” below the list shows which state counts as done, running, waiting or blocked.

AMW takes every p package through its states: draft → ready to start → running → handed in → in acceptance → ready to merge → merged → done. Alongside: blocked (question open), unclear (no final line), waiting for interactive, aborted, deferred. In Planning and the overview a p package shows like any task as running, waiting, blocked or done.
Tasks with `--paket agent` (the default) have none of these states – the task status applies to them as before.

**Approve what is ready to merge:** Below the list, “Ready to merge” shows every fully checked package: which files it changes (`diff --stat`) and the changes themselves to expand. On the PC, “Approve all” approves them all at once; in the terminal use `amw paket freigeben --alle` (package reviewer, lead or you). AMW then fetches exactly each package's state as branch `paket-A<number>` into the project and records “Prüfung C (AMW) + approval” and the merge OK; delivery runs through the chain as always. Afterwards the package is “merged” and “done”, and its workspace is free again.

**Bundle and deliver:** `amw paket buendeln --alle` (lead or you) puts the approved packages one after another on top of the current state – in a separate working folder, never in the live folder. AMW raises the version number (MINOR if a package brings something new, otherwise PATCH), writes the release notes from the packages' notes and runs the full test run through the run queue. If it is green, you get “Bündel X.Y.Z bereit” with the changed files, the release notes and the two commands to approve and deliver – only you or the lead approve the release. If a package does not fit on top of the others (conflict), it stays out and waits for you; packages that come “after” it stay out as well. What a project needs for this is in the project settings `version_datei`, `changelog_datei`, `gesamtlauf_befehl` and optionally `buendel_schritt` (follow-up step, e.g. building the web page). If a bundle's full test run stops before it ran, `amw paket buendeln --gesamtlauf buendel-X.Y.Z` starts it again for the same bundle. If a bundle is not delivered, its packages stay approved: the next `amw paket buendeln --alle` takes them along again without you approving them again.
fragen: What makes a good acceptance command?
One that checks exactly what the package should deliver, runs fast and is red today. A whole test run is too broad; a single new test or a small test class is ideal.

`--nach`: the package needs the result of the other task. `--nie-gleichzeitig`: the two get in each other's way, in either order. `--gleiche-ressource`: many packages share something (e.g. the same test database) – they get the same name and run one after the other.
A package waits for me after the check – but it is fine. How does it get into the merge list?

Some packages always go to you or the lead after the check first, for example the package type “test-schreiben” or a hint about outside access that turns out to be harmless when you read it. AMW keeps the checked state. Once you have read it and it is fine: `amw paket annehmen <no> --grund "what you read"` (lead or you). The package then appears under “Ready to merge” and is approved and delivered like any other.
A p package is stuck – how do I hand it to an interactive agent?

If it is “waiting for interactive”, “blocked”, “unclear” or “aborted”: `amw aufgabe aendern <no> --paket agent --agent <id>`. From then on the normal task status applies again; the states up to then stay in the planning log.
What does the package type “test-schreiben” do?

For packages that write a test for a change. Their acceptance command is naturally not red before the work; instead the new test must be red against the old state and green against the new one, and the lead reads it.

For packages that only write tests for existing, unchanged code. Such tests are honestly green against today's code – so AMW does not check “red against old” here, but: the package changes test files only, the tests run green, and at least one test really ran (skipped ones do not count). Afterwards the lead reads the tests and accepts the package (`amw paket annehmen`).
Why do I have to look at some packages before I approve them?

If a package changes code that runs online on the server (`web/*.php`), it shows “review first” in the list. “Approve all” skips it; you approve it on its own with “Reviewed – approve” (in the terminal `amw paket freigeben <number> --blick`). Check: new endpoints and their sign-in, outbound calls, shell calls, file and database access, and which data is output. Under Settings › Project only you decide whether a review is needed for server code only, for every package or never, and whether outbound calls stop a package or only show as a note. If a delivery changes server code, the release notes say “Server-Code geändert” (server code changed).
